existing_teaching.actual_text_excerpt:
<!-- teaching: CH01-GRAM-WEIGHT CH01-PAR-NEUT-WEIGHT -->

Neuter nominative and accusative are identical in each number. The genitive and dative endings match those of **fisc**. In the ordinary monosyllabic pattern, the nominative/accusative plural has **-u** after a short stem, but no ending after a heavy stem. A short vowel followed by one consonant gives the short pattern here; a long vowel or long diphthong, or a short vowel followed by two consonants, gives the heavy pattern. A doubled consonant counts as two. Thus **hof** has **hofu**, whereas **sǣd, gærs, cynn** have no added N/A plural ending. Vowel length and syllable weight are not the same thing.[5]

| Case | hof singular | hof plural | sǣd singular | sǣd plural |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nominative | hof | hofu | sǣd | sǣd |
| Genitive | hofes | hofa | sǣdes | sǣda |
| Dative | hofe | hofum | sǣde | sǣdum |
| Accusative | hof | hofu | sǣd | sǣd |

The heavy pattern also covers **lēoht, līf, gēar, dēor, anginn, lyft, weorc**. In **anginn**, apply the rule to the stressed stem **-ginn**, with **nn**. Plural forms of mass or abstract nouns do not automatically have the same sense as the singular; the vocabulary below marks those whose plurals are only for recognizing the morphology.

existing_teaching.actual_text_excerpt:
## 1. Principal parts and finite stems

<!-- teaching: NEW-U04-GRAM-STRONG-WEAK-CONTRAST -->

<!-- teaching: NEW-U04-GRAM-PRINCIPAL-PARTS-REFERENCE -->

<!-- teaching: NEW-U04-GRAM-INDICATIVE-SCOPE -->

The weak verbs already learned add a dental element in the preterite. A strong verb instead has a series of stems: the vowel of its present, singular preterite and plural preterite may differ. The **four principal parts** identify this series. They are conventionally listed as infinitive, singular preterite, plural preterite and past participle.

<!-- table: U04-PRINCIPAL-PART-POSITIONS -->

| Position | Function |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Infinitive | Names the verb and identifies the present stem. |
| 2. Singular preterite | Identifies the ordinary first/third singular preterite stem. |
| 3. Plural preterite | Identifies the stem used in all plural persons and in the second singular. |
| 4. Past participle | Completes the cited stem series; its syntax is not yet required. |

Thus drīfan, drāf, drifon, drifen display the Class I sequence ī : ā : i : i. Drāf and drifon are finite indicative forms. The infinitive and participle columns are **supplied citations**: they may be consulted, and their independent recall or use in infinitive, participial, perfect or passive constructions is not required here. A principal-part entry identifies a stem; the complete tables below identify the person and number.

Present indicative forms state present actions or conditions; preterite indicative forms state past actions or conditions. Every finite table in this unit covers those two tenses and all three persons in singular and plural. The two rare reference verbs in §5 are for recognition only.
existing_teaching.scope_and_gap: Actual prose explains a strong vowel series; the register calls it ablaut. A diachronic contrast with umlaut is still missing.

existing_teaching.actual_text_excerpt:
### c, g, and combinations

| Spelling | Sound | Supplied examples and limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| c | **k** as in *kit*, or **ch** as in *chin*. | **cuman**, “come”, begins with **k**. Both **c** letters in **cyrice**, “church”, are **ch**. |
| c before a front vowel | Often **ch**, but not invariably. | **cēlan**, “cool”, begins with **k**, despite **ē**. |
| g at the beginning | Hard **g** as in *go*, or consonant **y** as in *yes*. | **god**, “god”, has hard **g**; **giefan**, “give”, begins with **y**. |
| g elsewhere | Consonant **y**, or the continuous sound described below; some contexts retain hard **g**. | **dæg**, “day”, ends with **y**; **fugol**, “bird”, has continuous **g**. |
| sc | Usually **sh** as in *ship*. | **scip**, “ship”, has one **sh** sound; **frosc**, “frog”, instead ends with **s** followed by **k**. |
| cg; usually gg | The final sound of *bridge*. | **ecg**, “edge”. The supplied exception **docga**, “dog”, has a prolonged hard **g**. |
| ng | Usually as in *finger*, with audible **g**. | **lang**, “long”. In **sengan**, “singe”, **ng** instead has the sound at the end of *singe*. |

The front vowels **e, i, æ, y** help explain many **ch** and **y** pronunciations, but the next written letter is not a complete rule. Words and inflected forms have exceptions. Use the supplied sound for each example; do not turn every **c** before **e** into **ch**. In **cyrice**, keep all three syllables, including the final **e**.

proposed_outline.title: Reading a historical explanation
proposed_outline.purpose: Set optional scope; distinguish sound history, spelling, a paradigm alternation and reconstruction. Define vowel front/back and rounding in plain words; refer to the pronunciation guide rather than repeat it.

proposed_outline.title: Fronting and restoration
proposed_outline.purpose: Prepare the changes behind æ/a and why a following syllable can matter; state chronological and West Saxon limits.

proposed_outline.title: Breaking
proposed_outline.purpose: Explain a front vowel acquiring a second element in the relevant consonant environments; give a compact source-qualified rule and examples. Distinguish the letters ea/eo from a claim of identical origins.

proposed_outline.title: i-umlaut
proposed_outline.purpose: Explain anticipation of a following i/j, the later loss/change of that trigger, and surviving results in nouns, derivation, comparison and present singulars. Compare long and short results; avoid an unrestricted conversion table.

proposed_outline.title: Other origins of diphthong spellings
proposed_outline.purpose: Separate back mutation from breaking and palatal diphthongization; include a short paragraph on smoothing with an exactly sourced dialectal example if useful.
proposed_outline.open_source_need: A verified smoothing example may need an additive form route to an existing headword.

proposed_outline.title: Consonants and the order of changes
proposed_outline.purpose: Explain palatalization, selected exceptions produced by chronology, and gemination in plain articulatory terms. Distinguish consonant changes from changes in the following vowel.

proposed_outline.title: Vowel loss, syllable weight and contraction
proposed_outline.purpose: Connect historical final vowel loss and internal syncope with familiar paradigms; keep long vowel and heavy syllable distinct. Treat contraction as a bounded additional mechanism.

proposed_outline.title: Ablaut, inherited alternations and analogy
proposed_outline.priority: core distinction; short optional consonant note

actual_course_location.context: **Æ æ** is a single vowel letter. **Þ þ** (thorn) and **Ð ð** (eth) represent the sounds written *th* in modern English; the choice between the letters does not by itself distinguish the sounds of *thin* and *this*. This unit follows Cook's use of **ð**. His hooked **ę** is an editorial form of *e*, retained in such words as **męte** and **męnn**. A macron marks a long vowel or diphthong: **ā, ǣ, ē, ī, ō, ū, ȳ; ēa, ēo, īe**. Preserve the marks printed in each word; do not add them by analogy.[1]

actual_course_location.context: Neuter nominative and accusative are identical in each number. The genitive and dative endings match those of **fisc**. In the ordinary monosyllabic pattern, the nominative/accusative plural has **-u** after a short stem, but no ending after a heavy stem. A short vowel followed by one consonant gives the short pattern here; a long vowel or long diphthong, or a short vowel followed by two consonants, gives the heavy pattern. A doubled consonant counts as two. Thus **hof** has **hofu**, whereas **sǣd, gærs, cynn** have no added N/A plural ending. Vowel length and syllable weight are not the same thing.[5]

notation_policy: For the eventual learner master, bold every cited OE word, reconstructed historical example and letter/ending used as an object; italicize explanatory English terminology. Inventory every resulting bold span as an attested example, reconstruction, comparison, letter or fragment.

An asterisk in this appendix marks a reconstructed historical form, not an incorrect Old English exercise answer. Unit3 explicitly uses the same symbol for proposed errors, so state the local distinction.

Use an escaped literal star inside Markdown emphasis, for example **\*fōti**, only after the exact reconstruction and stage are source-verified. This string is a notation example, not an approved historical example.
A chronological arrow means developed into. Use plain beside or a colon for coexisting paradigm forms; do not imply that a singular historically changed into its plural.
Distinguish letter spellings from sound descriptions in words. No new IPA is needed for the proposed exposition; if one symbol is indispensable, define it once.
Retain Cook-baseline spellings and quantities, including ę, short geaf and unmarked feoh. A Fulk variant or added consonant dot needs an explicit normalization or comparison note.
Mark West Saxon, Anglian, earlier and later results where relevant. Do not present a chosen course reading convention as the only historically possible pronunciation.
Supply a meaning and the grammatical identity of every attested example, including citation-only forms; no independent recall is tested.

glossary_integration.existing_route_policy: Each attested example identifies exact surface, lemma, sense and printed headword entry. Homographs need the selected route, not just a successful string match.
glossary_integration.new_surface_existing_headword_policy: A useful additional inflection or dialect spelling may point to its existing glossary headword, with appendix-specific primary-source provenance and local gloss; absence from the frozen exact-form index is not itself a reason to reject it.
glossary_integration.new_lemma_policy: Prefer the familiar candidates here. If a necessary new attested lexeme is retained, give an explicit supplemental dictionary entry/access route without silently changing the frozen original acceptance records.
glossary_integration.reconstruction_policy: Reconstructed pre-OE stages, Gothic/Latin or modern comparanda, stem symbols and rule letters must be visibly labelled and supplied; do not register them as attested OE headwords.
glossary_integration.english_glossary: No new exercise tasks are proposed, so the original exercise-only English glossary scope remains unchanged.
